2007A16.goal: $a,b,c,d$ are random from $0$–$2007$ (half even, half odd). We want $P(ad-bc\text{ even})$. Only parities matter: $ad-bc$ is even exactly when $ad$ and $bc$ have the same parity.
2007A16.approach: $P(ad\text{ odd})=\tfrac14$, $P(ad\text{ even})=\tfrac34$; same for $bc$. Same parity: $\left(\tfrac14\right)^2+\left(\tfrac34\right)^2$.

steps.title: Each product
steps.explain: $0$–$2007$ has $1004$ evens and $1004$ odds, so each variable is odd with probability $\tfrac12$. $P(ad\text{ odd})=\tfrac14$.

solution: $ad-bc$ even iff both odd or both even: $\tfrac1{16}+\tfrac9{16}$.
2007A16.recognize: Parity of expressions in random integers: reduce each variable to odd/even with probability $\tfrac12$.

2007A17.goal: $75m=n^3$ with positive integers; we want the smallest $m+n$. $n^3$ must contain $3\cdot5^2$, so every prime in $n^3$ needs an exponent that is a multiple of $3$.

tools.name: Prime factorisation
tools.why: To make a cube we fill exponents up to multiples of $3$.

2007A17.approach: The smallest cube divisible by $75$ is $3^3\cdot5^3=15^3$. Then $m=\tfrac{3375}{75}=45$, $n=15$.

check.q: What is the smallest cube divisible by $75$?

2007A17.shortcut: Larger $n$ makes both $m$ and $n$ bigger, so the smallest $n$ wins.
2007A17.recognize: "$km$ is a perfect power": fill each prime's exponent up to the next multiple.

2007A18.goal: A plus-shaped $12$-gon with sides $4$ and right angles; $AG$ and $CH$ meet at $M$. We want $[ABCM]$. Put it on coordinates and find $M$.

tools.name: Coordinates
tools.why: Going around the cross with steps of $4$.

2007A18.approach: With the cross on a $12\times12$ grid, $AG$ runs $(4,12)\to(8,0)$ and $CH$ runs $(8,8)\to(4,0)$. They meet at $M=\left(\tfrac{32}5,\tfrac{24}5\right)$. Add $[ABC]=8$ and $[ACM]$.
2007A18.bridge: Coordinates, intersection, then split the quadrilateral.
traps: Assuming $M$ is the centre of the cross.
Ordering the quadrilateral's vertices wrongly in shoelace.
2007A18.recognize: Grid-shaped figures: coordinates make intersections and areas mechanical.

2007A19.goal: A brush of width $w$ paints both diagonals of a square of side $s$, covering half of it. We want $\tfrac sw$. The unpainted part is four isosceles right triangles, one on each side.

tools.name: Unpainted triangle
tools.why: An isosceles right triangle with hypotenuse on the side and height $h$ has area $h^2$.

tools.name: Height
tools.why: The triangle's apex sits where two stroke edges meet, $\tfrac{w/2}{\sin45^\circ}=\tfrac w{\sqrt2}$ from the centre.

2007A19.approach: Unpainted $=4h^2=\tfrac{s^2}2$, so $h=\tfrac{s}{2\sqrt2}$. Set $\tfrac s2-\tfrac w{\sqrt2}=\tfrac{s}{2\sqrt2}$ and solve for $\tfrac sw$.

steps.title: Solve
steps.explain: $\tfrac s2-\tfrac{s}{2\sqrt2}=\tfrac w{\sqrt2}$. Multiply by $2\sqrt2$: $s(\sqrt2-1)=2w$, so $\tfrac sw=\tfrac2{\sqrt2-1}=2\sqrt2+2$.

2007A19.bridge: Write the gap's height two ways.
solution: Unpainted: $4$ triangles of area $h^2$, total $\tfrac{s^2}2$, so $h=\tfrac{s}{2\sqrt2}$.
2007A19.shortcut: Estimate: half painted means a thick brush; $\tfrac sw\approx4.8$ matches (C).
traps: Taking the apex distance as $\tfrac w2$.
Computing the painted area as $2sw\sqrt2$ without the overlap.
2007A19.recognize: Painted strips: it's often easier to compute the unpainted pieces.

2007A21.goal: Cube (surface $24$) → inscribed sphere → inscribed cube. We want the inner cube's surface area. The sphere's diameter is the outer side and the inner space diagonal.

tools.name: Cube in sphere
tools.why: Opposite vertices are on the sphere.

2007A21.approach: Outer side $2$. Inner $s\sqrt3=2$, so $s^2=\tfrac43$ and surface $=6\cdot\tfrac43=8$.

steps.title: Diameter
steps.explain: $6s^2=24$, so the outer side is $2$; the sphere's diameter is $2$.

check.q: A cube has surface area $24$. Its side?

2007A21.bridge: Outer side = diameter = inner space diagonal.
2007A21.recognize: Nested cube–sphere–cube: side, diameter, space diagonal.

2007A22.goal: Three-digit terms whose digits shift along cyclically. We want the largest prime that always divides the sum $S$. Each digit shows up once in each place value.

tools.name: Place-value bookkeeping
tools.why: The hundreds, tens and units columns contain the same digits.

2007A22.approach: Every digit that appears as a hundreds digit also appears once as a tens and once as a units digit. So $S=(100+10+1)k=111k$ where $k$ is the sum of hundreds digits.

steps.title: Columns
steps.explain: The tens digits are the hundreds digits shifted one term along, and the units digits shifted two. All three columns have the same digit sum $k$.

steps.title: Prime factor
steps.explain: $111=3\cdot37$; $k$ can be anything, so the largest guaranteed prime is $37$.

2007A22.bridge: Each column sums to the same $k$.
traps: Thinking $k$ must be a multiple of something.
2007A22.recognize: Cyclic digit shifts: column sums are equal, so the total is a multiple of $111\ldots1$.

2007A23.goal: Count pairs $m\ge n\ge1$ with $m^2-n^2=96$. Factor as $(m-n)(m+n)=96$; the factors must have the same parity.

tools.name: Difference of squares
tools.why: Turns the problem into factor pairs.

2007A23.approach: $96$ is even, so both factors are even: $(2,48),(4,24),(6,16),(8,12)$. Each gives one pair with $n>0$.
2007A23.bridge: Count factor pairs of $96$ with both factors even.
2007A23.shortcut: Write $m-n=2a$, $m+n=2b$: $ab=24$ with $a<b$, and $24$ has $4$ such pairs.
2007A23.recognize: Differences of squares equal to $N$: factor pairs of $N$ with matching parity.

2007A24.goal: Circles at $A$ and $B$ (radius $2$), $O$ the midpoint with $OA=2\sqrt2$; tangents $OC$, $OD$ and the common tangent $EF$ bound region $ECODF$. Its area is the rectangle $ABFE$ minus two right triangles and two sectors.

tools.name: Angles at $A$
tools.why: $\triangle OAC$ is isosceles right; $AE\perp EF\parallel AB$.

2007A24.approach: Rectangle $ABFE$: $4\sqrt2\times2=8\sqrt2$. Remove triangles $OAC$, $OBD$ (area $2$ each) and sectors $CAE$, $DBF$ ($\tfrac\pi2$ each).

steps.title: Pieces
steps.explain: $OC=\sqrt{8-4}=2$, so $\triangle OAC$ is a right isosceles triangle with area $\tfrac12\cdot2\cdot2=2$ and $\angle OAC=45^\circ$. Sector $CAE$: $90^\circ-45^\circ=45^\circ$, area $\tfrac\pi2$.

check.q: What is the area of rectangle $ABFE$?

2007A24.shortcut: Curvy regions bounded by tangents: big polygon minus right triangles minus sectors.
2007A24.recognize: Regions between tangent lines and circles: rectangle/triangle pieces minus sectors.

2007A25.goal: Count $n$ with $n+S(n)+S(S(n))=2007$. Mod $9$ forces $3\mid n$, and size bounds limit $n$ to a short range.
2007A25.approach: Mod $9$: $3n\equiv2007\equiv0$, so $n\equiv0\pmod3$. With $1969\le n\le2007$, test the multiples of $3$.
2007A25.bridge: Use mod $9$ and bounds, then test a few candidates.
2007A25.shortcut: Mod $9$ cuts the candidates to about a dozen; checking them is quick.
2007A25.recognize: Equations with digit sums: mod $9$ plus a size bound.
